title: Existence, uniqueness, and maximal solution intervals
terms: initial-value problem; local existence; local uniqueness; Picard-Lindelof theorem; maximal interval of existence.

For y = F(t, y) with y(t ) = y , continuity of F near (t , y ) guarantees a local solution. A

local Lipschitz condition in y gives uniqueness; continuity of ∂F/∂y near the initial point is a
convenient sufficient condition. These are local conclusions, not promises of a solution for all
real t. Even polynomial right sides can produce finite-time blowup.
A maximal interval is the largest interval containing the initial time on which that solution
extends. When a uniqueness hypothesis fails, uniqueness may still hold in a particular problem,
so failure of the theorem is not itself a proof of nonuniqueness. To demonstrate nonuniqueness,
construct distinct solutions with the same initial condition and check them at the joining time.
The Picard–Lindelof theorem gives local existence and uniqueness for a continuous explicit
right side that is locally Lipschitz in the dependent variable: on a small rectangle, |F (t, y ) −

Separation gives y = (1 − 2t) on the branch fixed by the positive initial value. It blows

question.text:

For the differential equation y = 2ty/(t − 1), defined only when t ̸= ±1, the initial condition is
y(0) = 0. What is the maximal solution interval containing zero?
(A) R (B) (−∞, 1) (C) (−1, ∞) (D) (−1, 1) (E) {0}

solution.text:
Local uniqueness forces the zero solution on the connected time interval (−1, 1). Although
the function zero is bounded and can be written at every real time, the specified differential
equation is undefined at t = ±1. A solution interval containing zero cannot cross those
times. A finite maximal endpoint need not result from blowup of the solution itself.
